name: Anycast and BGP Routing
intent: Announce one IP prefix from many sites and let BGP carry each client to a site, then understand what that does to latency, failover, hijacks and DDoS.
scenario: A service announces the same /23 (192.0.2.0/23, origin AS 64500) from five cities: Los Angeles, New York, London, Singapore and Sao Paulo. Each client network is sent to whichever site its own ISP's BGP routers prefer. Then a site is withdrawn for maintenance, a rogue AS announces a more specific /24, and a flood arrives from a botnet.
problem: DNS-based geo routing steers users with a guess about where the resolver is, and it fails over only as fast as TTLs and resolver caches allow. For services that must be reachable at one address from everywhere (public DNS, CDN edges, DDoS scrubbing) you want the network itself to pick the nearest healthy site. But BGP is a policy protocol, not a latency optimiser: it does not know geography or RTT, a route change can move a client to another site in the middle of a TCP connection, withdrawing a route takes tens of seconds to propagate, and anyone who can announce a more specific prefix can steal your traffic.

howItWorks.title: Autonomous systems announce prefixes
howItWorks.text: The internet is about 75,000 autonomous systems (AS), each with a number such as AS 64500. Neighbouring ASes run BGP over TCP port 179 and send UPDATE messages: a prefix (192.0.2.0/23) plus attributes, notably the AS_PATH, the list of ASes the announcement has crossed. Each AS prepends its own number when it passes the route on, which also lets it detect loops (it rejects any path containing its own AS). A router forwards each packet by longest-prefix match against the routes it chose.

howItWorks.title: Anycast: the same prefix from many sites
howItWorks.text: Anycast is not a protocol, only a deployment: every site announces the same prefix with the same origin AS, usually through a local transit provider or an internet exchange. Each remote router now holds several paths to that prefix and keeps the best one (next step). Every ISP therefore ends up with a catchment of sites it sends to. A client does not choose, and nothing measures RTT: 'nearest' means 'preferred by BGP policy', which usually, but not always, correlates with geography.

howItWorks.title: Best-path selection decides the site
howItWorks.text: A router compares routes in a fixed order: highest local preference first (operators set it to prefer customer routes, which earn money, over peers, which are free, over paid transit: for example 200, 100, 50), then shortest AS_PATH, then lower origin type and MED, then eBGP over iBGP, then lowest IGP cost to the exit, and finally lowest router ID as the last tie-breaker. Because local preference comes before path length, a Seattle ISP whose upstream has New York as a customer route can be sent to New York although Los Angeles is 1,500 km closer.

howItWorks.title: Withdraw a route to drain or fail over a site
howItWorks.text: To take a site out, the site (or a health-checking agent next to it) withdraws the prefix, or the BGP session drops when the site dies. Neighbours then recompute and propagate, with path exploration and the 30 s or so MinRouteAdvertisementInterval pacing eBGP updates, so the whole internet settles in tens of seconds to a few minutes. If the box just dies with no BFD, the hold timer (90 s or 180 s by default) must expire first, and packets are black-holed meanwhile. Withdraw before maintenance, keep the site serving until traffic has left, then stop it.

howItWorks.title: Long connections are the cost
howItWorks.text: Routers are stateless about flows. When a route change moves a client to another site, its next TCP segment lands on a server that has never seen the connection and gets a RST. DNS over UDP and 100 ms HTTP requests simply retry, which is why anycast suits them. Long downloads, WebSockets and video sessions suffer, so operators keep routing stable (no flapping, avoid unnecessary path changes), use ECMP with consistent or resilient hashing inside a site so adding a server does not remap flows, drain by withdrawing and waiting, and increasingly use QUIC connection IDs or application reconnect logic.

howItWorks.title: Protect the announcement and absorb attacks
howItWorks.text: A more specific prefix always wins: a rogue AS announcing 192.0.2.0/24 captures traffic from every network that accepts it, whatever the AS_PATH. Defences are RPKI route-origin validation (a signed ROA states that AS 64500 may originate 192.0.2.0/23 up to a maxLength; validating routers drop invalid announcements), IRR-based prefix filters on customer sessions and your own /24 deaggregation where you can. The same catchment mechanics spread a DDoS: each botnet source reaches its own nearest site, so a widely distributed flood is split across all sites, while a concentrated one overwhelms a single site.

pros: One address works everywhere, with no DNS TTL or resolver-caching delay on failover
Usually sends clients to a topologically close site, and the network does it with no per-request logic
Spreads DDoS traffic across all sites by catchment, and each site has its own capacity
Single-packet protocols such as DNS survive route changes with no special handling
Failing a site is an operational act: withdraw the route and traffic moves
cons: BGP policy, not latency or geography, decides: some clients land on a far site and you cannot see it without measurement
Convergence takes tens of seconds to minutes, and a dead site with a slow hold timer black-holes traffic
Route changes can break established TCP connections mid-flow
Hard to control load: you steer with prepends, communities and selective announcements, and results differ per ISP
Needs your own AS and IP space (at least a /24 for IPv4), peering or transit at every site, and BGP expertise
whenToUse: Authoritative and recursive DNS, NTP and other UDP or short-request services
CDN and edge proxy fleets that terminate connections close to users
DDoS scrubbing and mitigation networks that need many sites sharing one address
Global entry points where DNS failover delay is unacceptable
whenNotToUse: A single region or a few servers: a regular load balancer and health checks are far simpler
Services with long-lived stateful connections and no reconnect or session-migration logic
When you need precise control over which user reaches which site: use DNS geo routing, latency-based routing or a global load balancer
When you cannot run a real BGP presence (own AS, prefix, multiple upstreams): then rent anycast from a CDN or cloud provider
pitfalls: Assuming anycast gives lowest latency: a customer route with a high local preference can send a user across an ocean
Announcing the prefix from a site whose service is down, because the BGP agent has no health check tied to the application, so traffic is black-holed
Withdrawing a route and stopping the service at the same instant: traffic keeps arriving for the convergence time
Flapping routes (a health check that toggles the announcement) causing repeated connection resets and route-flap damping at upstreams
Announcing a /24 from one site only and a /23 from the rest, so more-specific routing quietly defeats the anycast design
Not publishing ROAs, or setting maxLength too low or too high: too low makes your own deaggregated /24s invalid, too high lets a forged-origin hijack of a /24 stay RPKI-valid
A small site with a large catchment: it is the first to saturate in an attack, and withdrawing it just moves the flood to the next site

roles.label: Client network
roles.description: An ISP or eyeball network whose users send packets to the anycast address.

roles.label: BGP router / AS
roles.description: A network that learns routes, applies local preference and path length, and forwards by longest-prefix match.

roles.label: Anycast site
roles.description: A city where the service announces the shared prefix and serves traffic.

roles.label: Operator
roles.description: The team that withdraws and restores announcements.

roles.label: Rogue AS / botnet
roles.description: A network that announces a stolen prefix or sends flood traffic.

quiz.question: A DNS provider announces the same /24 from six cities. A resolver in Seattle is sent to the New York site although Los Angeles is closer. Its ISP reaches New York through a customer link. What most likely explains this?
options: Anycast measures round-trip time to each site, and the New York reading was wrong
The Seattle resolver cached an old DNS answer that still points at New York
The Los Angeles site announced a longer prefix than the other five sites did
BGP weighs local preference before path length, and customer routes rank very high
quiz.explanation: Anycast has no latency measurement: each ISP's BGP policy picks the site, and local preference outranks AS_PATH length. DNS caching is not involved, since there is one address everywhere.

quiz.question: An operator must take the Singapore anycast site out for maintenance. Which plan keeps user impact lowest?
options: Stop the service first, so that the health checks notice and remove the site
Withdraw the prefix, wait for traffic to drain, then stop the service
Stop the service and withdraw the route at the same moment, to save maintenance time
Announce a more specific prefix from the other four sites, to pull the traffic away
quiz.explanation: Routers keep sending packets until the withdrawal has propagated, which takes tens of seconds, so the service must keep answering during that time. Stopping first black-holes traffic.

quiz.question: A video company serves 30-minute live streams over long TCP connections from an anycast address at eight sites. During a routine route change at one transit provider, a few percent of viewers get connection resets and must reconnect. Which statement best explains the resets?
options: Anycast sites share TCP state, but the sync between the sites lags by a few seconds
The new site refused the packets because its BGP session was still in the hold timer
The new path ends at another site that has no state for that flow, so it sends a reset
The viewers' ISP dropped the packets because the AS_PATH had grown a little longer
quiz.explanation: Routers keep no per-flow state, so a changed route can deliver the next segment to a server that never saw the connection. Sites do not share TCP state, so the answer is not sync delay.
